newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish oil privatisation faces further hitch.
newsitem.headline: Turkish oil privatisation faces further hitch.

text.p: Turkey's seven-year-old lethargic efforts to privatise its oil companies may hit a further hitch despite recent government efforts to sell them off this year.
The sell-off requires the realistic pricing of petroleum products from refineries, based on a new formula drawn up by the energy ministry, officials and industrialists say.
But there is continuing uncertainty over whether or when related legislation will be passed by parliament.

The Automatic Pricing Mechanism (OFM) is designed to end the losses of the refineries -- state-run Tupras and private Atas -- and to raise profit margins of the petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi, they said.
"You cannot privatise companies which make losses," said Ugur Dogan, undersecretary at the energy ministry, which hammered out the OFM system.
"The mechanism is a must and an important prerequisite for the privatisation of Tupras and Petrol Ofisi," he told Reuters in an interview.
Turkey slated the two companies for privatisation in 1990 but has so far sold only 1.66 percent of Tupras and four percent of Petrol Ofisi to the public and employees.
"The decrees for the OFM are ready. But before implementing them, the special consumption tax (OTV) law, which governs the OFM, must be legalised," Dogan said.

A draft law on the tax was proposed to parliament in May during the short-lived rule of the previous government, which collapsed in June after dispute between the centre-right partners. It has since then been awaiting parliamentary action.
"The (present) government may make some modifications in the draft OTV law and maybe that is the reason why they are holding it at the parliament commission," a parliament official said.
He said he did not expect MPs to debate the draft soon.

The government has said it will open tenders in the first quarter of 1997 for partial sales of Tupras and Petrol Ofisi, but the official said if it cannot pass the tax law on time, it would face the dilemma of trying to sell a loss-making company.
The OTV law scraps about 10 existing taxes, duties and fees imposed on several goods and introduces a single tax on them.
Petroleum products are the biggest group of goods to be covered by the OTV, with a 68 percent share. The others are predominantly luxury items.
The automatic pricing mechanism will readjust government subsidies, taking into account the prices of crude oil and petroleum products in Italy -- the Mediterranean benchmark.

Dogan said the automatic pricing system would scrap two of the four existing taxes, including a special duty called AFIF, imposed on the refinery wholesale prices, and introduce two fixed taxes instead of the current proportional taxing system.
The 15 percent AFIF was imposed in 1989 to create funds to prevent refineries from making losses due to crude oil price fluctuations, but officials said it has failed to achieve the purpose.
Oil analysts say the government's losses from abolishing the AFIF may amount to $400 million a year, but add the cash-strapped government must dispense with it to save oil firms from losses.

"The government cannot further afford having losses in its oil firms in order to keep the AFIF in place. If it abolishes it, it will earn more in future," said one Istanbul-based official from a Western oil company.

According to the OFM, the fixed taxes will be determined either on a lira per tonne, or ECU per tonne basis. "Dollar per tonne or the inflation index are among the other options in order to take into account the lira's devaluation," Dogan said.

The OFM will use calculations based on Platt's Oilgram index, and the new scheme will allow local refinery wholesale prices to fluctuate within a certain band. "But consumers will not be affected by the fluctuations because the government can step in to adjust the two taxes accordingly," Dogan said.
Industry sources said the losses of the state refinery Tupras were about five trillion lira ($44.6 million) in the first nine months of 1996.

The only private refinery Atas, owned by Mobil /BP, Shell and private Tabas, stopped production in October, saying that its losses of $55 million for 1996 were caused by the existing pricing system and it would not resume operation until the government has adopted the OFM.
Retail petroleum prices are about 40 percent below international prices in Turkey and the difference is written off as loss on refineries.

"The government should either raise retail petroleum prices by 40 percent now to stop our losses or adopt the automatic pricing mechanism immediately," Ertugrul Tuncer, general manager of Turkey arm of Mobil/BP, told Reuters.
"The system will enable the refineries to earn more from their sales but the government's tax revenues will drop a bit."
Tupras operates four refineries and has a local market share of 86 percent, the remaining 14 percent belonging to Atas.
The government hopes to bring in $5 billion through privatisations this year, including partial sales of Turk Telekom and steel company Erdemir.
